newsitem.title: USA: U.S. disappointed at Honduran ruling on Francois.
newsitem.headline: U.S. disappointed at Honduran ruling on Francois.

text.p: The U.S. State Department voiced disappointment on Thursday at a Honduran judge's decision to turn down a U.S. request to extradite former Haitian police chief Joseph Michel Francois to face drug trafficking charges.
But spokesman Nicholas Burns said Washington hoped the decision would be reversed on appeal.

Honduran judge Marco Alvarado rejected the extradition request in Tegucigalpa on Wednesday and gave the United States three days to appeal or he would order Francois released. The U.S. Justice Department said it would appeal.
"We're very disappointed by the decision of the Honduran judge," Burns told a news briefing.
But, he added, "there is an appeal under way, and we are hopeful that appeal will overturn this decision, and that Michel Francois will face justice."

Honduran police backed by U.S. agents arrested Francois, the feared police chief of the Haitian capital Port-au-Prince during the 1991-1994 military government, on March 7 in San Pedro Sula. He was living there in exile after fleeing Haiti following the 1994 U.S. invasion that toppled the junta.

U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) officials had planned to bring him directly to Miami and into court, and were dismayed when Honduran legal authorities held up the operation as he was being escorted to the airport.

The U.S. indictment against Francois said he used his position as police chief to turn Haiti into a vast staging post to ship thousands of pounds (kilos) of cocaine and heroin to the United States in league with Colombian drug barons.
"This is a very bad guy," Burns said. "He was involved in narcotics. He was a major abuser of the human rights of the Haitian people. He does not deserve to go off scot-free."
